title: Melanosome Chemistry, Packing, and Exposure History as Potential Modifiers of Laser Iris Pigment Response: A Testable Hypothesis
content: Background: Human iris melanosomes are chemically heterogeneous. Surface-sensitive studies have identified an eumelanin-associated outer signature in selected human iris stromal granules, while other elemental-mapping findings challenge a universal core–shell model. Neither observation establishes a chemistry-dependent laser response in the human iris. Hypothesis: Baseline eumelanin/pheomelanin composition or surface state may predict a reproducible physical response after controlling for pigment amount, optical absorption, particle size, and local packing. Separately, the physical response to a later challenge may depend on whether a first exposure occurred. The latter effect must not be equated with chemical conversion without independent state measurements. Proposed tests: Ethically sourced donor-derived stromal melanosomes would undergo paired chemical, structural, and visible-wavelength optical characterization. Donor-held-out prediction would test added value of chemistry. Randomized sham-first versus exposed-first preparations, material-balance measurements, packing controls, and medium exchange would test exposure history and alternative explanations. Implications: The proposal distinguishes organelle-scale physical outcomes from visible iris color, pigment clearance, and ocular safety. A null chemistry effect would favor simpler optical and geometric models; a repeatable effect would justify mechanistic studies and human iris explant validation.
